User-vector interrupts can call more than one program depending on the value on the address bus from the device calling for the interrupt. The 68000 microprocessor system used in this experiment is setup to demonstrate the actions of autovector interrupts.

User-vectored interrupts are more complicated. They allow each of the 7 interrupts to call different programs. The device calling a user-vectored interrupt would set the appropriate interrupt line, leave the VPA low, and put an address on the address bus to indicate which user-vector for this interrupt to call.

The microprocessor then determines which interrupt number was requested and gets the address for that interrupt program from the interrupt's vector location. The program is run and control is passed back to the interrupted program which then continues its operation.

When a device calls an autovectored interrupt, the proper line on the encoder must be set low and a low sent to the VPA (Valid Peripheral Address) pin on the 68000. The VPA pin tells the microprocessor that the requested interrupt is an autovectored interrupt.

A "vector" in microprocessor terms is nothing more than an address value stored somewhere in memory. Vectors are normally stored in memory sequentially in what is known as a vector table. Vector tables are often referred to as jump tables because they tell the microprocessor where (in memory) to jump to.

Recall the interrupts are used to stop the microprocessor from executing one program, execute another, and then return to the original program. Interrupts come in a variety of types, both hardware and software. There are two main types of hardware interrupts: autovectored and user-vectored.

23. Using the oscilloscope set to measure DC, connect the CH1 probe to the RESET TP and the CH2 probe to the HALT TP of TPB3 on the PC130-468 card. Set the Time/Div to 1ms and both Volts/Div to 0.5V. Place the CH1 trace to the top half of the screen and the CH2 at the lower half.
Whenever the reset button is pressed, C6 is discharged; releasing the button allows C6 to charge again and the circuit reacts the same as if power had been initially applied.

With the F/F's set and reset pins low, they are effectively out of the circuit. This allows the low on the D input to be clocked through the Q output. This, in turn, drives the Q output high which is subsequently felt on the reset and halt pins of the 68000, disabling any halt of reset function.

The low on Q is felt across the reset and halt pins of the 68000, which are active low, resetting the system. After C6 charges through R8, current flow stops which puts a low on the set pin of the F/F.

The reset circuit contains a switch, a capacitor, a D-F/F, three resistors and three diodes. When power is applied to the system, C6 is not charged and a high is applied to the set pin of the F/F. With the set signal high and the reset signal low, the Q output goes high and drives the Q output low.

You have just examined the primary functions available from the 68000 keyboard. Other functions will be discussed as they become pertinent to the lesson.
READ COM : The read com function is used to read data from the serial port and store it in memory.
WRITE COM: The write com function is used to send data from memory to the serial port.
OUT: The out function is used to send data from memory to the parallel port.
IN : The in function is used to input data from the parallel port and store it in memory.

ADD/SUB: The add/sub functions allow you to add or subtract hexadecimal or decimal numbers. The edit and run keys determine which base you are using. After selecting a base, enter the first number, press either the yellow + or - key, enter the second number and press enter. The display will show the result.
COPY BLOCK: The copy block function allows you to copy a segment of memory to another location in memory.
CONVERT: This key allows you to convert from hex to decimal or decimal to hex. The edit and run keys indicate which operation, and are color coded in yellow.
<: The left arrow is a backspace key used to review or delete characters you have entered.
^: The up arrow is used as an up function in certain programs.
: The down arrow is used as a down function in certain programs.
STOP: The stop key is used to terminate certain operations depending on the program you are using.
FILL : The fill function allows you to fill specified regions of memory with the same exact data.

ENTER: The enter command is used to tell the microprocessor you have finished entering data or, to perform certain operations. The exact purpose of the Enter key depends on the program or operation you are using.
DISPLAY R.M.: The display register/memory function allows you to view and alter any contents of the internal registers. You must use the edit command, however, to edit the contents of memory.
EDIT: The edit function allows you to change the contents in memory. This is how programs are manually entered into the 68000 trainer.
RUN: The run function allows you to begin a program stored in memory.

The alphanumeric keys provide all the hexadecimal symbols you will need for programming. The function keys are used to perform operations such as looking at the contents of various registers, running programs, etc. Each of these keys will now be examined.

All of the cards have Test Points to accommodate the measurement of different system signals. Now that we have examined each of the cards, let's set up the trainer.

Examine the PC130-404 card (Keyboard and Display). This card contains two major sections: the Keypad and the Display. The card is mounted on a separate chassis to prevent damage to the card and for ease of operation. It should be placed directly in front of the NIDA 130A Test Console.

Examine the PC130-401 card (I/O). This card contains two major sections: the Parallel Data Port and the Serial Data Port. This card attaches to the PC130-404 card using the long 20-pin ribbon cable and is installed in PC3 on the NIDA 130A Test Console.
Examine the PC130-403 card (Chip Select/Memory). This card contains two major sections: the Address Decoder (chip select) and Memory (ROM and RAM). This card attaches to the
PC130-401 card using the short 20-pin ribbon cable and is installed in PC2 on the NIDA 130A Test Console.

Examine the PC130-468 card (68000 Microprocessor). This card contains three major sections: the Microprocessor, Clock and Timing circuits and the Data Bus Buffers. This card attaches to the PC130-403 card using 50-pin ribbon cable and is installed in PC1 on the NIDA 130A Test Console.

The NIDA 68000 Microprocessor Trainer is comprised of four circuit cards. Three of these cards attach directly to the NIDA 130A Test Console and the fourth card is placed in front of the console. Three ribbon cables are used to connect the circuit cards together and provide the appropriate signals.

In this experiment you will become familiar with the NIDA 68000 Microprocessor Trainer and observe the various signals being sent to and from the microprocessor. The first set will be to learn how to set up the system and to learn what each circuit card contains.

Processor Function Code (FC0, FC1, FC2): These signals are outputs that indicate the mode and addressing space currently being used. These codes are valid when the address strobe signal is active (low).

Valid Peripheral Address (VPA): The VPA signal is an input to the microprocessor from devices using the enable signal. This signal tells the microprocessor that the address is valid for some given device. The VPA signal is also used with the interrupt signals for different types of interrupts.
Enable (E): The enable signal is used as a clocking signal for certain peripheral devices specifically designed to be used with the 68000. This signal is active high.

Halt (HALT): The halt signal causes all operations within the microprocessor to stop after the current cycle, set all tri-state devices to high impedance output (no connection to bus) and set all control signals to inactive. This signal is bi-directional, active low, and used with the reset signal to restart the system.
A hardware reset requires a low input to this pin. A software reset will output a low to this pin which can be sent to other devices to reset them as well. This signal is active low.

Reset (RESET): The reset signal is used in conjunction with the halt signal to reset the entire microprocessor system. Used by itself, this signal can reset certain sections of the processor. The reset signal is bi-directional; you can reset the system with hardware or software.

Suppose you are running a program on a computer and you move the mouse. An interrupt request is generated and sent to the processor. The processor identifies the new position of the mouse, and then returns to the program you are using.

Interrupt Control (IPL0), IPL1, IPL2): Interrupts are signals that tell a processor to stop one program, execute another and then return to where it left off in the original program. An example of a device using an interrupt is a mouse.

Bus Grant Acknowledge (BGACK): This signal from the requesting device informs the microprocessor that it has taken control of the system. The processor will now prevent other devices from taking over the system. This signal is active low.

Bus Grant (BG): The bus grant signal is generated by the processor in response to the bus request signal. It informs the requesting device that it can take control of the system at the end of the processors current cycle. This signal is active low.

Bus Request (BR): The bus request signal is used to allow other devices to take control of the address, data, and control buses. This signal asks the microprocessor for permission to take over the system. This signal is active low.

Data Transfer Acknowledge (DTACK): This input to the processor is from devices attached to the data bus. The signal tells the processor that either the data on the bus has been read or that it has been written. This prevents incorrect data from being transferred to or from the processor. This signal is active low.

Upper and Lower Data Strobes (UDS, LDS): These strobes are used with the read/write signal when a data transfer is being performed. The 16 data lines from the processor are split into two groups of eight and sent to different memory chips. The upper and lower data strobes indicate which bits are being read.

Read/Write (R/W): The read/write signal indicates to devices the type of data transfer being performed in the current cycle. A high level on this pin means the device is reading data, while a low indicates a write operation.

This signal is tri-stated. The line above the "AS" indicates that the condition is true if the signal is low. A high signal on this line indicates an invalid address. This low condition is referred to as an active low pin. Active low pins are common in any microprocessor.

Address Strobe (AS): The address strobe signal is used to inform other devices that the information on the address bus is valid. This ensures that devices don't attempt to read an address before the CPU has installed a complete address on the bus.

The control bus consists of 20 pins (27 if you include power, ground and the system clock) used to regulate when things occur in the CPU. Let's examine each pin and its function. NOTE: Pin 18 and 31 have no connection and so are not included in the control bus.

The 68000's longword capability essentially makes it a 32-bit processor. Data transfer is regulated by signals from the control bus and is asynchronous. This means that the communicating device does not operate on the same clock signal that the CPU is operating on.

The data bus works in conjunction with the address bus to send or receive data to memory or I/O. If byte size data (8 bits) is accessed, it will be read from either D0-D7 or D8-D15, not both. If word data (16 bits) is accessed, data will be read from D0-D15. Longwords require two reads of D0-D15.

A clear way to visualize the difference between the two buses is that you can take information (read) from the address bus, but you cannot send information (write) to it. The data bus, conversely, allows information to be written to and read from it.

The data bus in the 68000 occupies pins 58 through 68 and 1 through 5. They are assigned as D0 through D15. While the address bus is uni-directional, the data bus is bi-directional. This allows the data bus to simultaneously carry a composite signal from ROM, RAM, the keyboard and other I/O devices.
PIN CONFIGURATION

The address lines allow the 68000 to connect up to 16 megabytes of memory to the system. In applications where more memory is needed, other techniques and additional IC's can be used to increase this amount.

The address bus is also tri-stated so, if needed, the 68000 can remove its signals from the bus and allow another processor to control the system signals. Tri-state devices use the third logic state (high impedance) to allow multiple devices to use the same line.

It should be noted that while, for the most part, IC identification labels break out similarly, the actual meaning of the numbers and letters used in the label may be vastly different from one IC to the next. Always consult the appropriate data book for the part number legend.
The last field of the label (12) indicates the maximum speed the microprocessor will operate. The 12 tells us that the microprocessor used by the NIDA 68000 Trainer, operates at
12 MHz. Other versions of the 68000 operate at 8, 10, 16, 20, 25 and 33 MHz.

Following the unique circuit description is a letter field, in our example FN. This is the package type. As you probably know, IC's come in different physical forms and pin arrangements. The FN indicates, for Motorola coding, a Quad Pack. Package types will be discussed in detail further in this lesson.
Sometimes the unique circuit description includes letters which indicates the particular technology used in the construction of the IC, such as CMOS.

The second field (68000) of the label is the unique circuit description. This indicates the IC's actual function. Other Motorola microprocessors are 68008, 68010, 68020, 68030, 68040 etc. Each of these microprocessors have their own special features and are, for the most part, not fully compatible with the 68000.

The MC at the beginning of the label is the standard prefix which indicates the manufacturer that produced the IC, in this case Motorola. Motorola has licensed the rights of this IC to other companies which, in that case, would carry a different manufacturer prefix.
Look at the identification label of the 68000 microprocessor used in the NIDA 68000 Trainer. A lot of information can be obtained just from this label alone.
